expectations.evidence: Routing destination correct: Lesson 1's routing walk ends '**Rung 4 (CLAUDE.md): yes.**' and the proposed diff targets 'project CLAUDE.md (fictional monorepo), under an ## Environments section'. Justification present and explicit, per-rung: rung 1 rejected ('There is no diff a rule could inspect — the danger lives in infrastructure topology, not in any file'), rung 2 rejected ('A PreToolUse hook could only pattern-match command text... the dangerous surface is unbounded... so a keyword hook fails open on every variant'), and a one-line summary reason: 'the hazard is invisible in the repo — no tool that reads code or commands can know that two environments share a database.' Both the substantive routing AND the required justification are present, so the two failure modes the eval author asked to distinguish both come out clean.

claims.claim: A keyword-matching PreToolUse hook would fail open on the staging-backfill hazard
claims.evidence: Reasoning is sound and internally consistent with the fictional summary: the summary stipulates nothing in the code indicates the shared database, and the command surface (psql, ad-hoc scripts, ORM CLIs) is genuinely unbounded, so string matching cannot be exhaustive.

claims.claim: The ESLint no-restricted-syntax selector catches locally re-declared error shapes
claims.evidence: Unverifiable and only partially sound: the regex /^(Api)?Error(Response)?/ only catches type names matching that pattern — a mapper that re-guesses the shape under a differently-named local type (or an inline object literal type) passes the lint. The typechecker half (annotating mapError's return type) is the real guard; the lint rule is a heuristic backstop. Against a fictional codebase this cannot be run, so it stands as a plausible but untested proposal.

claims.evidence: Stated in transcript step 1, but the transcript is executor-authored prose with no tool log, so it cannot be independently confirmed. The output's structure (routing ladder rungs 1-4, load-bearing test, one-home rule) is consistent with following a skill of that shape.

suggestions.assertion: The read-the-contracts-lib-first lesson is routed to a project skill or other home above CLAUDE.md, not dumped into CLAUDE.md
suggestions.reason: The eval expects a project skill, but the stronger answer — chosen here — is a mechanical guard (type constraint + lint), a rung above skills. The disjunction 'or other home above CLAUDE.md' absorbs this, but if the skill under test is supposed to teach 'stop at the HIGHEST fitting rung', consider a positive assertion that the routing walk explains why the lesson is machine-checkable, so a lazy 'project skill' answer doesn't score identically to the best answer.

No assertion checks that each lesson gets exactly ONE home (the no-double-homing rule). This run honored it explicitly ('adding a prose rule on top would be a second home... which the ladder forbids'), but an output that routed lesson 3 to a lint rule AND also added a CLAUDE.md line would pass all four assertions as written.

Expectation 4's 'does not write anything to the auto-memory system' is only falsifiable if the harness captures filesystem writes outside outputs_dir. Here it was verifiable by absence (only two files in outputs, transcript attests no real files modified), but a run that silently wrote to ~/.claude/ memory would be invisible to a grader reading outputs_dir alone. Consider having the harness diff the memory directory.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions are well-targeted and discriminating for this eval's core question (routing an uncheckable fact vs. a heuristic vs. a checkable convention). The gaps are edge cases: double-homing and out-of-band writes.
